table.brief: Two sibling sub-columns under "Price" where one holds short numbers ($12) and the other long qualifiers ("$12 per seat per month, billed annually")

understanding.purpose: A procurement/comparison reference: pick a plan (row) and read its price, how it is billed, seat minimums, contract and support terms. It is scanned vertically by plan and compared horizontally by attribute.
understanding.reading: Reader anchors on column 1 (Plan), reads the bold price, then the billing-terms sentence that explains it, then the three short constraint/attribute columns (seats, contract, support) as a quick checklist. So the eye moves plan → price pair → terms strip, and column 3's long prose is the one cell that must wrap.
groups: cols 2+3 (Price group): 'List price' is the number, 'Billing terms' its explanation — they must stay adjacent under the merged 'Price' header and be read as a pair
cols 4,5,6 (Minimum seats / Contract / Support): same role — short attribute values in a checklist strip; they should share a similar, compact rhythm even if their headers are narrower than one line
col 1 (Plan) stands alone as row identity and needs a clean, uninterrupted edge
keep_intact: Plan names (Education = 75px) — never split a row identifier
Currency amounts ($12, $45) and the price column header 'List price' (67px)
Short contract/support values and their header words if any scroll budget exists
may_wrap: Billing terms prose (490px one-line) — the natural flexible column; 2–6 lines are acceptable and absorb row-height growth
'Minimum seats', 'Contract', 'Support' headers into two lines if width forces it
Billing-terms header word 'Billing' only as a last resort

preferred.name: r3C
preferred.note: Explores the opposite trade: push width into billing terms (210 → text 189, 3 lines) so every row stays short and reads as a single band, accepting 637px total. Attribute columns stay at their no-split minimums so nothing wraps or splits, and the reader scrolls horizontally to a compact, evenly-rhythmed checklist rather than a tall ragged one.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Spend the budget where row height is actually created: Billing terms 170→220 (189px of text) so the longest sentence breaks into ~3 lines instead of 5, collapsing rows to a near-uniform ~83px. Plan 96 and List price 88 keep identity and the $ amounts intact and adjacent. Seats/contract/support at 100/105/125 let 'Minimum seats' wrap to two lines but keep every value ('25', 'Annual', '24/7') on one line, preserving the checklist rhythm. Accepts 365px overflow as the price of a real comparison grid.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Keeps the whole reading core — plan name, bold price and the complete billing-terms sentence — inside the first 360px (96+60+175 = 331, so billing ends before the box edge), while compressing the attribute strip to minimums so total drops to 602. Billing gets text 154 → 4 lines, cutting row heights versus lean-min; the attribute checklist is one short scroll away rather than lost in a long one.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Compromise between r1A's overflow and r1B's paragraph stack: keep the table near r1A's total (634 vs 626) but rebalance — terms 170→150 is still comfortably above the 86px 'commitment' word so no mid-word splits, and trimming seats/contract/support to 95/95/110 brings the whole attribute strip 60px closer to the visible box. Rows stay in the 83–106px band.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Moderated r0C: Billing 160 still lets Plan+Price end at 344px inside the first screen, while Minimum seats gets a full one-line 130px and Contract/Support get 110/130px so the checklist is comfortable when reached. Total 714px; more scroll than 625, but far less cramped on the right.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: New idea: give Minimum seats and Contract their exact natural one-line widths (109, 123) so those columns never wrap a value or a header, and give Support 150 so only its longest phrase breaks. Terms stays at 170 (4–5 lines) rather than being inflated, because with the attribute columns at natural width the row heights are already capped by terms alone. Total 736 — more scroll than r1A but every column is internally clean.

bad.name: r1B
bad.note: The narrowest no-split table: keep Billing at 107 (the 'Billing' floor), widen List price from 58 to 88 to stop its header wrapping, and hold the other columns at their word-safe floors. Total 562px, 202px overflow; all words stay intact, but billing rows remain tall.
bad.why: Billing terms is squeezed to 107px, producing 8-line cells and a 1082px-tall table; the prose column becomes a narrow ribbon that is hard to scan, and the table still overflows.

bad.name: r3A
bad.note: Every column except billing terms is set to its unbreakable-minimum width (Plan 96, List price 62 so the header wraps to two lines, Minimum seats 87, Contract 84, Support 100); all remaining budget goes to billing terms. Total 557px — the smallest table that keeps every word and value intact. Billing prose wraps to 5 lines, a deliberate height-for-width trade, and the 197px scroll is the shortest of any no-split layout.
bad.why: Billing terms is only 128px, forcing 6-line cells and an 826px-tall table while still overflowing by 198px; it is both scroll-heavy and vertically bloated.

rationale: r3C is the best phone compromise: its first three columns (Plan, List price, Billing terms) total 366px, so the core pricing information is almost exactly one viewport wide while the secondary columns scroll. Giving Billing terms 210px keeps the longest cells to three lines and the table to 593px high without mid-word splits. The 60px List price column still holds $12/$45 intact and wraps its two-word header cleanly; the tight secondary columns are acceptable because they are secondary and wrap at word boundaries.

general: Allocate width by information role: prose columns need the most space; identifier and price columns need just enough to stay intact.
On phones, try to keep the primary reading path (row label plus key values) within one viewport; let secondary columns scroll.
A two-word header wrapping at a space is usually preferable to squeezing a prose column into 4–6 lines or splitting words.
Avoid designs that both overflow and remain very tall; that is the worst of both worlds.
specific: Billing terms is the only long-prose column and drives row height; 210px gives three lines, while 170px or less forces four to five and 107px forces eight.
Plan needs 96px and List price about 60px to keep 'Enterprise' and '$12' intact; the List price header can wrap cleanly at the space.
Minimum seats, Contract and Support can be 87/84/100px because their headers and data wrap at word boundaries and they are secondary.
r3C's core Plan + Price width is 366px, almost exactly the 360px viewport; r2A's core is 404px.

tradeoffs: r2A is 46px shorter and has only one wrapped header, but it is 97px wider and pushes the core price columns further off-screen; r3B is 35px narrower but 70px taller. The choice depends on whether horizontal scroll or vertical length costs the reader more.
uncertain: Whether the 60px List price column feels too tight in practice; whether Support's data needs more than 100px; whether a three-line Billing terms cell is acceptable or two lines are required. A designer could reasonably prefer r2A for its cleaner headers and shorter rows.

critique.good: Plan and List price stay readable, the Price pair remains adjacent, and the table almost fits the 360px frame (9px over), so there is no horizontal scroll.
critique.problems: The right-hand checklist is destroyed: 'Minimum seats', 'Contract' and 'Support' become vertical letter stacks, values split mid-word (101 splits), rows grow to 292–362px, the tallest cell is 15 lines and the table is 2231px tall. Nothing can be compared at a glance.
critique.cause: The 38px widths leave only 17px of text, far below the 63–79px longest words in those columns; the 100px Billing column also cannot hold 'commitment', so the damage compounds.

critique.good: No mid-word splits; Plan, List price, Billing terms and Minimum seats are legible in the first 360px, the Price pair reads as a unit, and row heights (36–199px) are reasonable.
critique.problems: The List price and Billing terms headers wrap unnecessarily, Billing at 107px gives only 86px of text so prose runs 6–8 lines and rows reach 199px, and Contract/Support are completely offscreen. Scrolling right loses the Plan labels.
critique.cause: 58px List price is below its 67px one-line content; 107px Billing is the no-split floor for 'Billing' but still narrow for 490px of prose; the 533px total overflows by 173px, hiding the last two columns.

critique.good: Publication-quality grid: no header wraps, no mid-word splits, tallest cell 3 lines, table only 500px tall; Plan, List price and Billing terms are beautifully readable.
critique.problems: At 925px it is almost three phone widths wide (565px overflow). The first screen shows only Plan, List price and part of Billing; the seat/contract/support checklist is far right, and scrolling there loses row identity.
critique.cause: Widths were set to one-line ideals: 250px Billing, 130px Minimum seats, 144px Contract, 216px Support. The total ignores the 360px viewport; the luxury widths buy little because Billing already reads in 2–3 lines at about 180px.

critique.good: The Plan → List price → Billing terms run reads cleanly: identity column is uninterrupted, the bold $ amounts sit right beside their explanation, and at 170px the terms cell settles into 4–5 lines with no mid-word splits. Row heights 83–129 are the most even of the three.
critique.problems: The whole attribute strip (Minimum seats / Contract / Support) is pushed outside the box — only a sliver of the next header ('Mi…') shows at the right edge, which is visual noise and hides half the table's purpose. Rows of 106–129px are still tall for a comparison grid.
critique.cause: 96+88+170 = 354px of the 359px budget is consumed by the three left columns, so cols 4–6 (87/84/100 = 271px) fall entirely outside the visible 360px; the 170px terms width is what sets the 4–5 line, 106–129px rows.

critique.good: The only design that gets the fourth column (Minimum seats) into the first scroll page, and it sits closest to the theoretical minimum table width (562px vs. 359 available), so the reader scrolls least. Zero mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Catastrophic vertical rhythm: rows range 60–199px, the tallest cell is 8 lines, and the table is 1082px tall — it stops reading as a grid of comparable rows and becomes a stack of paragraphs. 'Minimum seats' header wraps while its values are single digits, wasting a wrapped header on a 2-character column.
critique.cause: The 107px Billing terms column (86px of content) is narrower than the unbreakable word 'commitment' (86px), so every sentence is broken at ~86px into 6–8 short lines; that single width dictates every tall row.

critique.good: Cleanest type: no header wraps at all, terms at 160px holds 5 lines max, and the wider 130/110/130 attribute columns give the checklist strip breathing room.
critique.problems: Overflows the most (355px) while still showing only Plan/Price inside the box — so the extra 90px spent on seats/contract/support bought nothing visible or useful, since those values ('25', 'Annual', '24/7') are short. Tallest cell 5 lines, rows up to 129px.
critique.cause: Width was added to cols 4–6 (130/110/130), whose content one-lines are only 109/123/195px, instead of to col 3, whose 490px one-liner is the only real driver of row height; total 715px vs. r1A's 626px for the same 5-line worst cell.

critique.good: Cleanest left edge: Plan at 96 holds 'Education' on one line, and the Price pair sits adjacent with all seven headers on a single line. Row heights stay lowest of the three (max 3 lines, table 547px tall), so rows read as compact bands.
critique.problems: Still overflows by 375px, and the three attribute columns (seats/contract/support) are pushed entirely out of the 360px box — the reader sees plan, price and billing terms but never the checklist. It is also the most wasteful: billing terms gets 220px (text 199) for prose that reads fine at ~150, while cols 4–6 sit at 100/105/125 — near but below their one-line needs (109/123/195), so Support values still wrap for no gain.
critique.cause: Col 3 is over-allocated at 220 while cols 4–6 are given generous but insufficient widths; the sum is 735 because no column was compressed to its unbreakable minimum (87/84/100).

critique.good: Narrowest of the three (635) and it is the only one that shows a sliver of 'Minimum seats' inside the box, hinting at the attribute strip. Plan column again intact, no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Worst proportion: narrowest yet tallest (756px, 5-line cells, rows 106–129). Billing terms at 150 (text 129) shreds the prose into 4–5 short lines, and cols 4–6 at 95/95/110 are below even the unbreakable-word widths for 'Minimum seats' (66) and 'Support' (79) plus values, so those columns are both cramped and still off-screen. It buys no fit and pays in height.
critique.cause: Width was spread thin across all six columns: col 3 squeezed to 150 without shrinking cols 4–6 to their true minimums, so the 275px overflow remained while wrapping exploded.

critique.good: Best internal proportions: billing 170 (text 149) gives readable 4–5 line prose, and cols 4–6 at 109/123/150 match their one-line content widths so those headers and values stay on one line with no splits. Consistent rhythm across the attribute strip.
critique.problems: Widest table (737) with the largest overflow (377), and the entire attribute strip is off-screen, defeating the checklist role. Table is also 686 tall. Support at 150 is still short of its 195 one-line need, so some support values wrap anyway — paying width without getting the full benefit.
critique.cause: Cols 4–6 were given their full one-line widths (382px combined, more than the whole 360px box) on top of a 170px billing column; the six widths were never reconciled against a total budget.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r1B.why: Plan names and prices scan cleanly, and the seat counts are visible, but narrow billing terms create tall rows and frequent wrapping. Later columns require scrolling.

ref_auto.why: Plan, price and seat counts are easy to compare, but billing terms wrap heavily and the contract column begins at the viewport edge.

r3B.why: The wider billing column keeps phrases readable and rows reasonably compact while retaining plan names and prices at first sight. Seat counts sit at the viewport edge, and later columns require scrolling.

r2A.why: Billing terms have comfortable line lengths, but their text runs beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to finish reading several rows.

r3C.why: Plan names, prices and billing terms form a readable first view, with moderate wrapping. Minimum seats and the remaining columns require scrolling.

ref_equal.why: Although all columns fit, plan names, headers and ordinary words split across lines throughout, making both scanning and comparison difficult.

raw.unsure: The supplied views do not show the full widths or wrapping of the off-screen columns in A–E, so their horizontal scrolling cost and overall balance cannot be judged completely.

ref_equal.why: All columns fit, but plan names, headers and ordinary words split repeatedly. The narrow billing column makes rows exceptionally tall and comparisons difficult.

r1B.why: Plan names and prices are easy to scan, but billing terms wrap into many short lines. The viewport cuts through the minimum-seats column, and the remaining columns require scrolling.

r3C.why: Plan names and both price columns fit in the viewport, with billing terms wrapping into readable phrases and rows staying reasonably compact. Minimum seats, contract and support require scrolling.

ref_auto.why: Plan, price and minimum seats are visible together, which supports comparison. Billing terms wrap heavily, however, and the viewport cuts into the contract column.

r3B.why: Billing terms have comfortable line lengths and the rows read clearly, but the viewport cuts through minimum seats, leaving several columns to the right.

r2A.why: Plan names and list prices are clear, and billing terms wrap moderately. The viewport cuts through the billing text itself, so readers must scroll to finish even the visible price group.

raw.unsure: The supplied images do not show the full width of the wider tables, so I cannot judge the hidden columns or the total scrolling distance. C favors readable pricing; D brings minimum seats into the initial view.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
